citeAs: Amini, A., Gabriel, S., Lin, S., Koncel-Kedziorski, R., Choi, Y., and Hajishirzi, H. (2019). MathQA: Towards Interpretable Math Word Problem Solving with Operation-Based Formalisms. NAACL 2019.
creator: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, Hannaneh Hajishirzi (University of Washington, Allen Institute for AI)
description: MathQA is a large-scale dataset of 37,200 math word problems with corresponding multiple-choice options and aligned operation programs. It significantly enhances the AQuA dataset by providing fully-specified operational programs using a new operation-based representation language. The dataset covers multiple math domain categories including Geometry, Physics, Probability, Gain-Loss, and General problems.
name: MathQA
publisher: University of Washington / Allen Institute for AI
rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 3 validators reviewed each annotation; at least 2 out of 3 validators had to rank the operation program as valid for it to be selected.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Expert evaluation of 500 problems showed 92% of annotations are valid. Agreement between expert validation and crowd-sourcing validation was 87%. Alignment validation accuracy was 94.64% across categories. For categorization, human annotator agreement was 84% and their agreement with the model was 74.5%.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Figure Eight (https://www.figure-eight.com) — a custom dynamic annotation platform built on top of Figure Eight was used for crowdsourcing annotations.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators were provided with a problem description, a list of operations related to the problem category, and a list of valid arguments. They iteratively selected operations and arguments until the problem was solved. The platform dynamically calculated intermediate results after each operation submission. Annotators were restricted to select only from valid arguments (numbers in the problem, constants in the problem category, and previous calculations). Programs were only accepted if they included some numbers from the problem and whose final calculation was very close to the correct numeric solution. Annotators were randomly evaluated through pre-defined test questions and had to maintain an accuracy threshold to continue annotating.
rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that the AQuA dataset (source of problems) contains significant noise including problems with incorrect solutions, problems unsolvable without brute-force enumeration, and rationales with few or none of the required solving steps. The paper also notes that the categorization strategy may be noisy due to using only one mathematical interpretation for each domain-specific n-gram (e.g., 'square' or 'cube' can refer to geometry or exponential operations). The paper also mentions that models may exploit dataset biases through pattern-matching rather than learning logical reasoning.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was constructed by taking problems from the AQuA dataset (GRE- and GMAT-level math word problems) and annotating them with formal operation programs using crowdsourcing. Problems were first categorized into math domains using term frequencies, and then crowd workers used a dynamic annotation platform to align problems with operation programs. An automatic dynamic programming approach was also experimented with but not included due to noise.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw source data is the AQuA (AQUA-RAT) dataset by Ling et al. (2017), which contains over 100K GRE- and GMAT-level multiple-choice math word problems with rationales.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset omits high-order polynomials and problems where solutions are entirely non-numeric. The representation language does not cover all operations (e.g., factorization is not defined). Sequence problems requiring pattern understanding are currently unsolvable. The dataset only covers a subset of solvable problems from AQuA. Human performance significantly exceeds model performance, indicating remaining challenges.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Annotation expansion was performed: closely similar problems were found using Levenshtein distance (threshold of 4 words in edit distance), numeric values were replaced with generic numbers, and annotations were expanded to cover more problems from the AQuA dataset. The dataset was randomly split into 80/12/8% training/dev/test problems.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems from AQuA were filtered for solvability: problems with no words, sequence problems, problems requiring options to solve, non-numeric problems, and near-duplicates were identified. Math problems were categorized into domains using term frequencies (n-gram lexicon). Annotation expansion was performed by finding closely similar problems using Levenshtein distance with a threshold of 4 words in edit distance, replacing numeric values with generic numbers, and expanding annotations to cover more problems.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance interpretable automatic math word problem solving, which could benefit educational applications and automated tutoring systems. The operation-based formalism provides an extra layer of supervision that can reduce the influence of statistical bias in datasets.
rai:dataUseCases: Training and evaluating neural models for math word problem solving; developing interpretable math problem solvers that map problems to operation programs; research on logical reasoning over natural language; semantic parsing of math word problems.
